headline: Deer Island Ledge on the Last Ebb: Bass on Live Mackerel, Flounder Working the Flats
subhead: Mid-summer has the harbor's bass locked to structure by day and feeding hard at first and last light — here's where I'm putting the boat this week.
body_markdown:
Every morning this week I've had the same argument with myself at the dock: harbor islands, North Shore rocks, or run south to Plymouth. This week the harbor wins, and it's not close. The bait's stacked on the Deer Island ledge, the current's still got some teeth in it before the neap softens things up, and the bass have settled into the pattern I expect out of early August — deep on structure through the heat of the day, up on the pogies and mackerel at first light, last light, and after dark.

I've been starting at the Deer Island Light drop-off, working the edge where the channel falls from 15 feet to 30 on the last two hours of the ebb into dead low. Live mackerel and pogies on a fish-finder rig, 20-pound fluorocarbon leader, just enough weight to hold bottom without killing the bait's action. That drop is a highway for forage getting pushed out of President Roads, and the bass are sitting right on the lip waiting for it to spill over. Nothing enormous — mostly 26 to 34 inches, with a couple of overslot fish that came unbuttoned before I got a hand on them — but it's been a consistent bite, not a fluke morning. Same program works Spectacle Island's north ledge on the push of the flood, though I've had better luck there with a swimming plug worked slow over the rocks at first light than with bait.

If you'd rather stay shallow and light-tackle, Nahant is fishing the way it should in August. The rockpile pockets between the causeway and East Point are holding bass that slide up into two and three feet of water after dark chasing pogies pinned against the boulders. A black Sluggo on a 3/8-ounce weighted hook, or a Redfin swimming just under the surface, worked slow through the wash — that's the ticket. I had three fish over 30 inches out there Tuesday night in under an hour, then it went dead quiet for the rest of the tide. That's the nature of the rocks right now: short, sharp windows tied to the tide change, and if you're not there for it, you're just casting at empty water.

Gloucester and Cape Ann are holding mackerel schools thick enough that you can find them by the birds working before you ever mark them on the sounder, and the bass are shadowing those schools around the outer ledges off Rockport and Straitsmouth. Jig the mackerel on small diamond jigs for bait or bring a few home for the pan, then switch to a bucktail or umbrella rig and work the same water — the bass have been mixed right in, sitting under the bait balls in 25 to 40 feet. It's not a blitz, it's a working pattern, and the fish have been there for anyone willing to make the run out past the harbor mouth.

South of the city, Plymouth and Duxbury Bay have flounder fishing that's been steady and underrated all summer. Sandworms and clam strips on a simple spreader rig, fished on the flats at the top of the warm afternoon tide, are still putting fish in the bucket — nothing that'll win a tournament, but a solid meal and an easy day for anyone who wants to get off the rocks for a stretch. Scituate's had bluefish showing wherever peanut bunker have pushed up into the harbor mouth, and when those blues find the bait it turns into fast, violent topwater fishing for twenty minutes at a time — small Kastmasters and Deadly Dicks worked fast across the surface, no leader needed to be subtle about it, just keep your fingers away from their teeth when you unhook them.

We flagged last week that conditions in this zone would hold stable with no big thermal shift coming, and that's exactly how it's played — no cold-water surprises, no sudden bait crash, just the same warm, settled mid-summer read carrying through. That stability is why the pattern's been so readable: bass down deep on the ledges by day, up shallow on the rocks and drop-offs during the low-light windows, bluefish trailing whatever bait concentrates.

The tide range is narrowing into the neap over the next couple days, and that's going to change how I fish the harbor by the weekend. Softer current means less push over structure, which means I'll be going lighter — smaller jigs, slower retrieves, more patience letting the bait sit instead of relying on the current to do the work. The bridges and channel edges around Deer Island and the Chelsea River mouth tend to hold the strongest remaining current through a neap cycle, and that's where I'd put my time after dark this weekend if the bite up top goes quiet. Cod and haddock chances remain a deeper-water game right now — Stellwagen's edge and the offshore ledges off Cape Ann are the play if you want bottom fish, working jigs and diamond jigs tight to structure in 100-plus feet where the water stays cool enough to hold them through the summer.

If I had one trip to make this week, it's the Deer Island ledge on the last two hours of the ebb, live mackerel down deep, switching to a bucktail on the drift once the tide goes slack. The bait's there, the structure's there, and the fish have been showing up on schedule. Just don't expect it to stay easy if that neap tide takes the current out of it — that's when this bite gets fussy, and you'll need to slow everything down to keep drawing strikes.
